_work.title: Hildegard of Bingen — Scivias and Liber Divinorum Operum Illuminations
_work.blurb: The illuminated visionary manuscripts of Hildegard of Bingen (1098–1179), Benedictine abbess, theologian, composer, and doctor of the Church. Her two major illustrated works — Scivias (Know the Ways, c. 1151) and Liber Divinorum Operum (Book of Divine Works, c. 1163–73) — contain some of the most extraordinary cosmological imagery of the medieval period: an egg-shaped universe of concentric spheres, mandala-like diagrams of the Trinity, a cosmic man standing in the center of creation, and elaborate angel-hierarchies. The Scivias illuminations survive primarily through a 1927 hand-made facsimile (Eibingen Abbey) of the lost Rupertsberg Codex.

entries.title: Hildegard of Bingen — Scivias, First Illumination (c. 1150)
entries.summary: The first illuminated miniature from Hildegard of Bingen's Liber Scivias Domini (c. 1150), the opening image of the foundational illustrated visionary manuscript. Hildegard composed Scivias (Know the Ways of the Lord) between 1141 and 1151 at the Disibodenberg monastery, dictating her visions to the monk Volmar and her nun Richardis von Stade. The Rupertsberg Codex — for which these illuminations were likely made under Hildegard's personal direction — was evacuated to Dresden during World War II and is now lost; it is known through a 1927 hand-painted facsimile held at Eibingen Abbey.

entries.title: Hildegard of Bingen — 'Das Weltall' (The Universe), Scivias, c. 1165
entries.medium: manuscript illumination (1927 facsimile of lost original)
entries.summary: The iconic 'Universe' illumination from the Hildegardis-Codex (Scivias), depicting the cosmos as a great egg-shaped form surrounded by flames and encompassing concentric rings of elements, seasons, and winds. This egg-shaped cosmological diagram corresponds to Scivias I.3 and represents one of Hildegard's most distinctive contributions to medieval cosmography — a vision of the universe as a living, structured whole governed by divine harmony. The original Rupertsberg Codex is lost; this reproduces the 1927 hand-painted facsimile (Eibingen Abbey). From the Yorck Project digitization.

entries.title: Hildegard of Bingen — 'Der mystische Leib' (The Mystical Body), Scivias, c. 1165
entries.medium: manuscript illumination (1927 facsimile of lost original)
entries.summary: Illuminated page from the Scivias Codex showing 'The Mystical Body' (Der mystische Leib) — a vision from Hildegard's Scivias depicting the Church as a mystical body animated by the Holy Spirit. Hildegard's visions frequently collapse distinctions between cosmic and ecclesial bodies; the Church as Body of Christ maps onto the same harmonic structures as the cosmos itself. From the 1927 Eibingen facsimile via the Yorck Project.

entries.title: Hildegard of Bingen — 'True Trinity in True Unity', Scivias, c. 1165
entries.medium: manuscript illumination (1927 facsimile of lost original)
entries.summary: Illuminated page from the Scivias Codex depicting 'The True Trinity in True Unity' (Die wahre Dreiheit in der wahren Einheit) — a key Trinitarian vision from Scivias II.2. Hildegard depicts the Trinity through a series of concentric rings: a brilliant sapphire-blue center (the Son), a gold ring (the Father), and an enveloping fire (the Holy Spirit). This diagrammatic approach to Trinity theology — using concentric forms rather than figurative representation — is characteristic of her cosmological mode of vision. From the 1927 Eibingen facsimile via the Yorck Project.

entries.title: Hildegard of Bingen — 'Motherhood from Spirit and Water', Scivias, c. 1165
entries.medium: manuscript illumination (1927 facsimile of lost original)
entries.summary: Illuminated manuscript page from the Scivias Codex showing 'Motherhood from Spirit and Water' (Mutterschaft aus dem Geiste und dem Wasser), a 12th-century Romanesque vision illustration from Hildegard's Scivias. Hildegard's visions of generation and creation are characteristically pneumatological — the Holy Spirit as a maternal, generative force moving through the created world. From the 1927 Eibingen facsimile of the lost Rupertsberg Codex, via the Yorck Project.

entries.title: Hildegard of Bingen — Six Days of Creation, Scivias, c. 1152
entries.summary: Illuminated manuscript painting depicting God's six days of creation of the world, from Hildegard of Bingen's Scivias tradition. Shows divine creation of Earth, Heaven, and Adam in characteristic 12th-century Romanesque style, with strong use of azure blues and gold. Hildegard's Genesis visions in Scivias Part I merge cosmogony with theology: the creation of light, the firmament, and the first human are simultaneous with the formation of the moral and spiritual order.

entries.title: Hildegard of Bingen — Choirs of Angels, Scivias I.6 (fol. 38r), c. 1150
entries.summary: Manuscript illumination from Hildegard of Bingen's Scivias, Book I Vision 6, depicting the hierarchical choirs of angels (folio 38r of the Rupertsberg manuscript). A high-resolution scan (3,487 × 4,085 px) of one of Scivias's most distinctive angel-hierarchy visions. Hildegard's vision of the angelic orders draws on the Pseudo-Dionysian celestial hierarchy (Seraphim, Cherubim, Thrones, Dominions, Virtues, Powers, Principalities, Archangels, Angels) but visualizes it in her characteristic fiery, spinning mandala form. Vision 6 of Scivias Book I, 'The Armies of Angels.'

entries.title: Scivias, Codex Salisburgensis X,16 — Independent Manuscript Witness, c. 1150
entries.summary: A page from the Scivias manuscript preserved in the Codex Salisburgensis (Salzburg Codex X,16), an independent manuscript witness to Hildegard's visions separate from the Rupertsberg Codex. The Salzburg codex provides important evidence for the early reception and transmission of Hildegard's visual program beyond Rupertsberg — showing that the illuminations were copied and circulated in the decades following composition. Held at the Salzburg Museum / Stiftsbibliothek Salzburg.

entries.title: Celestial Jerusalem after Hildegard's Scivias — Lachèze Diagram (1863)
entries.summary: A schematic diagram of the Celestial Jerusalem based on Hildegard of Bingen's Scivias Book III visions, drawn by Pierre Lachèze for his 1863 French translation (Lyon Municipal Library, SJ A 402/865). Hildegard's vision of the Celestial Jerusalem in Scivias III.2 describes a fortified city of angelic orders and virtues, which Lachèze renders here as a hierarchical architectural plan. The Celestial Jerusalem vision is the culminating diagram of the Scivias cycle, matching the cosmic and ecclesial architecture of the earlier visions.
